claims.claim: ESG stands for environmental, social, and governance: a set of factors used to assess a company beyond conventional financial metrics. Environmental covers a firm's impact on nature and its exposure to climate risk (emissions, resource use, waste); social covers relationships with people and society (labor, human rights, community, diversity); governance covers how the firm is run (board structure, ethics, executive compensation, transparency, shareholder rights).

ESG ratings from different providers diverge substantially. A 2022 peer-reviewed study by Berg, Kolbel, and Rigobon found the average correlation among six major raters was about 0.54, far below the roughly 0.99 correlation between the major credit-rating agencies, so the same firm can receive very different ESG scores depending on the rater.

The study decomposed the divergence into three sources: measurement (different data and indicators for the same category, ~56% of divergence), scope (different sets of categories, ~38%), and weight (different importance assigned to categories, ~6%). It also found a 'rater effect' in which a rater's overall view of a firm colors its category-level assessments.

The IFRS Foundation's International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) issued IFRS S1 (general sustainability-related financial disclosures) and IFRS S2 (climate-related disclosures) in June 2023, effective for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2024. IFRS S1 and S2 build on and consolidate the TCFD recommendations and the SASB Standards; from 2024 the IFRS Foundation took over monitoring of climate disclosures previously done by the TCFD, which was disbanded.

The ISSB/IFRS standards focus on investor-oriented financial materiality: information about sustainability risks and opportunities that could reasonably affect a company's cash flows, access to finance, or cost of capital. This 'single materiality' (outside-in) view contrasts with the 'double materiality' approach.

The EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) requires large and listed companies to report sustainability information under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS, developed by EFRAG); the first companies applied the rules for financial year 2024, reporting in 2025. The ESRS use double materiality, which combines financial materiality (how sustainability issues affect the company) with impact materiality (how the company affects people and the environment).

GRI (Global Reporting Initiative) runs an independent, multi-stakeholder standard-setting process and its GRI Standards are the most widely adopted globally; GRI emphasizes an organization's impacts on the economy, environment, and people (an impact, inside-out orientation), distinct from the investor-focused financial orientation of the ISSB.

ESG is politically contested. In the United States the SEC adopted climate-related disclosure rules in March 2024, stayed them in April 2024 amid litigation, and in March 2025 voted to end its defense of the rules; by 2026 the SEC had moved toward rescinding them. Many U.S. states have passed 'anti-ESG' legislation, while proponents defend ESG as material risk information. The field is also criticized for greenwashing (overstating environmental or social performance).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether ESG belongs in investment and corporate decision-making at all
positions: Proponents: ESG factors capture financially material risks and opportunities (e.g., climate exposure, labor practices, governance failures) and improve long-term accountability and disclosure.
Critics: ESG politicizes investing, may conflict with a narrow reading of fiduciary duty to maximize financial return, imposes reporting cost, and rests on inconsistent measurement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as an ongoing policy and legal dispute. The lesson attributes both positions and adjudicates neither, and gives no investment advice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Exact correlation figure for ESG rating divergence
positions: Berg/Kolbel/Rigobon (2022) report an average pairwise correlation of about 0.54 across six raters (range roughly 0.38-0.71).
Other studies using different raters and samples report different ranges.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites the peer-reviewed 2022 figure, attributes it, and frames divergence qualitatively (same firm, very different scores) rather than treating any single number as universal.
